finding: The opening calls bone markers routine, but the bone section individualizes them and cites KDIGO against routine collagen turnover markers in CKD. This wording could turn selective testing into a standing diversion panel.
evidence: KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline, https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/KDIGO_CKD_MBD_Guideline_r6.pdf, recommendation 3.2.4 suggests against routinely measuring collagen synthesis or breakdown markers in CKD G3a–G5D; this page's bone section also says there is no universal diversion-only interval.

edit.old: The tests are routine (serum creatinine, BMP or CMP, vitamin B12 and bone markers), but the surveillance schedule and the thresholds for action are reconstruction-specific.
edit.new: Serum creatinine with eGFR and a BMP or CMP anchor surveillance when indicated; B12 testing and bone assessment depend on the reconstruction, CKD stage and clinical risk.

finding: The page upgrades NICE's post-cystectomy follow-up protocol from 'consider' to an unqualified recommendation in the renal section. Preserve the guideline's strength and its combined imaging/GFR wording.
evidence: NICE NG2 recommendation 1.6.2, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng2/evidence/appendix-a-summary-of-evidence-from-surveillance-pdf-6725567342, says to consider using a follow-up protocol with upper-tract imaging and GFR estimation at least annually after radical cystectomy.

edit.old: NICE recommends at least annual GFR assessment and upper-tract monitoring after radical cystectomy; early postoperative and abnormal results need more frequent assessment.
edit.new: NICE advises considering a post-cystectomy follow-up protocol with upper-tract imaging and GFR estimation at least annually; early postoperative and abnormal results may warrant more frequent assessment.

finding: The renal comparison relies on 2014–2015 cohorts and misses a 2026 synthesis relevant to diversion choice and upper-tract surveillance: renal outcomes were similar, but uretero-intestinal strictures were more frequent with neobladder. The pooled estimate is observational and should be qualified.
evidence: PMID 42287878; DOI 10.1016/j.urolonc.2026.05.017, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42287878/. Meta-analysis of 14 retrospective cohorts found no significant eGFR or ESRD difference between conduit and neobladder; uretero-intestinal stricture RR 2.58 (P=0.01), with heterogeneity and selection bias.

edit.old: This CKD-selected cohort is distinct from Nishikawa's unselected series and should not be pooled with it; it does not establish that continent diversion is safe in every patient with reduced renal reserve.
edit.new: This CKD-selected cohort is distinct from Nishikawa's unselected series and should not be pooled with it; it does not establish that continent diversion is safe in every patient with reduced renal reserve. A [2026 meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42287878/) of 14 retrospective cohorts found comparable long-term renal outcomes for ileal conduit and neobladder, but more uretero-intestinal strictures with neobladder (RR 2.58); heterogeneity and selection bias limit causal conclusions.

finding: NICE's annual post-cystectomy protocol is presented as an unqualified recommendation and changes 'B12 and folate' into 'B12 or folate.' Both the recommendation strength and the paired tests should match the guideline.
evidence: NICE NG2 recommendation 1.6.2, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng2/evidence/appendix-a-summary-of-evidence-from-surveillance-pdf-6725567342, says to consider a protocol monitoring for metabolic acidosis and B12 and folate deficiency at least annually.

edit.old: NICE recommends at least annual monitoring for metabolic acidosis and B12 or folate deficiency after radical cystectomy.
edit.new: NICE advises considering a post-cystectomy follow-up protocol with at least annual monitoring for metabolic acidosis and both B12 and folate deficiency.

finding: The 'three classic derangements' table presents hyponatremia as a general bowel-diversion effect, although the characteristic sodium-chloride loss is the jejunal conduit syndrome already described below. This blurs the segment-specific differential.
evidence: PMID 6429449; DOI 10.1002/jso.2930260307, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6429449/, describes jejunal conduit hyponatremia and hypochloremic acidosis from sodium-chloride loss into urine, with potassium and urea absorption. The page's segment table separately labels this jejunal pattern.

edit.old: | **Hyponatremia** | Sodium loss across bowel mucosa, especially with high urine output | Less frequent than acidosis | Assess severity, chronicity, volume status and cause; avoid an automatic salt prescription or rapid correction |
edit.new: | **Hyponatremia** | Sodium-chloride loss is characteristic of a jejunal urinary segment; in other diversions, investigate additional causes, including gastrointestinal losses | Segment-specific rather than a general bowel-diversion signature | Assess severity, chronicity, volume status and cause; avoid an automatic salt prescription or rapid correction |

finding: The ileal/colonic table makes hypokalemia part of the default acid-base signature, even though the cited review calls it less frequent and this page correctly warns that hyperkalemia can occur. The wording could bias treatment toward potassium-containing alkali.
evidence: PMID 21687576; DOI 10.1155/2011/764325, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3113422/, abstract says hypokalemia occurs less frequently than hyperchloremic acidosis; the page's line 63 warns of hyperkalemia in ileal/colonic diversion.

edit.new: Hyperchloremic **non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis**; potassium may be low, normal or high

finding: The bone paragraph turns a plausible acid-buffering mechanism into a stated cause of long-term adult fractures. The population study shows an association, while a 2024 systematic review finds multiple possible contributors and heterogeneous BMD results.
evidence: PMID 30865566, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30865566/, matched observational cohorts found fracture HR 1.48 after diversion; PMID 38365091, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38365091/, review of 12 studies/496 patients found reduced BMD in only six studies and identifies age, sex, BMI, acidosis and renal function as possible contributors.

edit.old: Bone serves as a buffer for excess acid; over years to decades, this manifests as decreased bone mineral density, growth failure in pediatric patients, and increased fracture risk in adults.
edit.new: Bone buffering is one mechanism by which chronic acidosis may contribute to demineralization and pediatric growth effects; adult fracture risk after diversion is observed, but its cause is multifactorial.<sup>[[20]](#ref20)[[21]](#ref21)</sup>

finding: The cited diversion review calls diarrhea the most bothersome complaint, not the most frequent; it also limits steatorrhea to larger small-bowel resections. The current two-sentence description makes both outcomes sound universal after ileal harvest.
evidence: PMID 21687576; DOI 10.1155/2011/764325, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3113422/, abstract calls diarrhea 'most bothersome'; section 3 says fat malabsorption/steatorrhea occurs only when larger portions of small intestine are resected.

edit.old: Diarrhea is the complaint patients report most often after urinary diversion.<sup>[[33]](#ref33)</sup> When a substantial length of preterminal (terminal) ileum is resected for the diverted segment, bile-acid resorption is impaired; unresorbed conjugated bile acids reach the colon and draw in water and sodium, and the depleted bile-acid pool also reduces fat absorption, producing steatorrhea.<sup>[[33]](#ref33)</sup>
edit.new: Diarrhea can be a particularly bothersome complaint after urinary diversion.<sup>[[33]](#ref33)</sup> Distal ileal harvest can allow bile acids to reach the colon and cause watery diarrhea; with more extensive small-bowel resection, depletion of the bile-acid pool can also impair fat absorption and cause steatorrhea.<sup>[[33]](#ref33)</sup>

finding: The cholestyramine instruction lacks two safety decision points in a page centered on acidosis and renal function: extensive ileal resection can make bile-acid sequestration worsen steatorrhea, and renal insufficiency or volume depletion raises concern for hyperchloremic acidosis. It also omits the spacing needed to avoid binding other oral medicines.
evidence: Cited diversion review https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3113422/ gives the 4 g twice-daily to 8 g twice-daily regimen. Canadian BAD guideline https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6985689/ Statement 12 conditionally suggests against bile-acid sequestrants after extensive ileal involvement/resection because steatorrhea may worsen (very-low-certainty evidence; extrapolate cautiously to diversion). Current Questran label https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=362ddd91-a63f-4ec6-841a-75785dd208c8 warns of hyperchloremic acidosis in renal insufficiency/volume depletion and advises other drugs at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after.

edit.old: Management starts with cholestyramine, a bile-acid-binding resin, at a starting dose of 4 g twice daily, increased gradually to 8 g twice daily as needed; long-term, high-dose use carries a risk of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
edit.new: For persistent suspected bile-acid diarrhea, first assess resection length, steatorrhea, hydration and other causes. In selected patients, cholestyramine may start at 4 g twice daily and increase gradually to 8 g twice daily; it can worsen steatorrhea after extensive ileal resection. Give other oral medicines at least one hour before or four to six hours after cholestyramine, and monitor bicarbonate and electrolytes when renal insufficiency or volume depletion increases acidosis risk; prolonged use can also impair fat-soluble vitamin absorption ([BAD guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6985689/); [Questran label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=362ddd91-a63f-4ec6-841a-75785dd208c8)).

finding: The section headed 'A Note on Liver Function Tests' also contains hyperammonemic encephalopathy and bile-acid diarrhea, so the heading hides a relevant bowel complication. A broader heading preserves all teaching while making the section navigable.
evidence: The cited review, PMID 21687576, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3113422/, treats diarrhea under bowel dysfunction/malabsorption rather than liver testing; the page itself places diarrhea at lines 152–156 beneath its LFT heading.

edit.old: ## A Note on Liver Function Tests

finding: The annual lab framework can be read as applying a bowel-acidosis BMP to an isolated catheterizable stoma. The linked appendicovesicostomy page and AUA/SUFU discussion explicitly distinguish a channel without augmentation from bowel-incorporating reservoirs.
evidence: AUA/SUFU 2021 NLUTD guideline Statement 58 discussion, https://www.auanet.org/documents/Guidelines/PDF/NLUTD.pdf, says an isolated continent stoma without augmentation lacks the electrolyte/acid-base risks of augmentation and annual evaluation without a BMP suffices for that indication; linked docs/04-surgical-techniques/04b-bladder-reconstruction/appendicovesicostomy.mdx states the same.

edit.old: A framework for stable long-term follow-up; adapt to the reconstruction, renal reserve and applicable guideline:
edit.new: Use this laboratory framework for bowel-incorporating reconstruction or another renal-risk indication, adapting cadence to the operation, renal reserve and applicable guideline. An isolated catheterizable channel without augmentation does not itself require an annual BMP for bowel-related acid-base risk.

finding: The annual table omits folate even though NICE's post-cystectomy protocol includes annual B12 and folate assessment. The table should distinguish that NICE protocol from the EAU B12-specific advice.
evidence: NICE NG2 recommendation 1.6.2, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng2/evidence/appendix-a-summary-of-evidence-from-surveillance-pdf-6725567342, includes monitoring for B12 and folate deficiency at least annually after radical cystectomy; EAU functional follow-up, https://uroweb.org/guidelines/muscle-invasive-and-metastatic-bladder-cancer/chapter/followup, says B12 should be measured annually after cystectomy with bowel diversion.

edit.old: | Vitamin B12 (MMA selectively if indeterminate) | Annual after cystectomy with bowel diversion; individualized for other ileal procedures | B12 status; interpret metabolites with renal function |
edit.new: | Vitamin B12 and folate (MMA selectively for indeterminate B12) | If following the NICE post-cystectomy protocol, test both at least annually; EAU advises annual B12 after cystectomy with bowel diversion; individualize for other ileal procedures | B12 and folate status; interpret B12 metabolites with renal function |

finding: The NICE bibliography points readers to recommendation 1.6.1, which only offers follow-up; the detailed annual imaging, GFR, acidosis, B12 and folate protocol is recommendation 1.6.2.
evidence: NICE NG2 recommendations 1.6.1–1.6.2, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng2/evidence/appendix-a-summary-of-evidence-from-surveillance-pdf-6725567342, separate the general follow-up offer (1.6.1) from the considered protocol and annual tests (1.6.2).
